questions.problem: A quadratic equation in the variable $x$ with real coefficients has a root $x=\frac{\sqrt{2}\text{i}}{2}.$ Given that the coefficient of ${x}^{2}$ in the equation is $6$, find the equation.
questions.worked_solution:
Since the quadratic equation has real coefficients and  $x=\frac{\sqrt{2}\text{i}}{2}$ is a root, its conjugate  $x=-\frac{\sqrt{2}\text{i}}{2}$ must also be a root. Therefore, using the zero product property, we can write a quadratic equation with the required roots as follows:

$$
(x-\frac{\sqrt{2}\text{i}}{2})(x+\frac{\sqrt{2}\text{i}}{2})=0
$$

Multiplying out the parentheses and simplifying gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}-{(\frac{\sqrt{2}\text{i}}{2})}^{2} & =0 \\ {x}^{2}-\frac{2}{4}(-1) & =0 \\ {x}^{2}+\frac{1}{2} & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

This equation has roots $x=\pm \frac{\sqrt{2}\text{i}}{2},$ but the coefficient of ${x}^{2}$ is not $6.$ Therefore, to find the desired equation, we multiply the equation above by $6.$ This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}6({x}^{2}+\frac{1}{2}) & =0 \\ 6{x}^{2}+3 & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: A quadratic equation in the variable $x$ with real coefficients has a root $x=-3-2\text{i}.$ Given that the coefficient of ${x}^{2}$ in the equation is $5$, find the equation.
questions.worked_solution:
Since the quadratic equation has real coefficients and $x=-3-2\text{i}$ is a root, its conjugate $x=-3+2\text{i}$ must also be a root. Therefore, using the zero product property, we can write a quadratic equation with the required roots as follows:

$$
(x-(-3-2\text{i}))(x-(-3+2\text{i}))=0
$$

By expanding the parentheses, we can write the equation in standard form as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}-x(-3+2\text{i})-x(-3-2\text{i})+(-3-2\text{i})(-3+2\text{i}) & =0 \\ {x}^{2}+3x-2x\text{i}+3x+2x\text{i}+9-4{\text{i}}^{2} & =0 \\ {x}^{2}+6x+9+4 & =0 \\ {x}^{2}+6x+13 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

This equation has roots $x=-3\pm 2\text{i},$ but the coefficient of ${x}^{2}$ is not $5.$ Therefore, to find the desired equation, we multiply the equation above by $5.$ This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}5({x}^{2}+6x+13) & =0 \\ 5{x}^{2}+30x+65 & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: A quadratic equation in the variable $x$ with real coefficients has a root $x=\sqrt{3}+\text{i}.$ Given that the coefficient of ${x}^{2}$ in the equation is $2$, find the equation.
questions.worked_solution:
Since the quadratic equation has real coefficients and $x=\sqrt{3}+\text{i}$ is a root, its conjugate $x=\sqrt{3}-\text{i}$ must also be a root. Therefore, using the zero product property, we can write a quadratic equation with the required roots as follows:

$$
(x-(\sqrt{3}+\text{i}))(x-(\sqrt{3}-\text{i}))=0
$$

By expanding the parentheses, we can write the equation in standard form as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}-x(\sqrt{3}+\text{i})-x(\sqrt{3}-\text{i})+(\sqrt{3}-\text{i})(\sqrt{3}+\text{i}) & =0 \\ {x}^{2}-x\sqrt{3}-x\text{i}-x\sqrt{3}+x\text{i}+3+\sqrt{3}\text{i}-\sqrt{3}\text{i}-{\text{i}}^{2} & =0 \\ {x}^{2}-2\sqrt{3}x+3+1 & =0 \\ {x}^{2}-2\sqrt{3}x+4 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

This equation has roots $x=\sqrt{3}\pm \text{i},$ but the coefficient of ${x}^{2}$ is not $2.$ Therefore, to find the desired equation, we multiply the equation above by $2.$ This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}2({x}^{2}-2\sqrt{3}x+4) & =0 \\ 2{x}^{2}-4\sqrt{3}x+8 & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Since the quadratic equation has real coefficients and $x=\frac{1}{2}+\sqrt{3}\text{i}$ is a root, its conjugate $x=\frac{1}{2}-\sqrt{3}\text{i}$ must also be a root. Therefore, using the zero product property, we can write a quadratic equation with the required roots as follows:

$$
(x-(\frac{1}{2}+\sqrt{3}\text{i}))(x-(\frac{1}{2}-\sqrt{3}\text{i}))=0
$$

By expanding the parentheses, we can write the equation in standard form as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}-x(\frac{1}{2}-\sqrt{3}\text{i})-x(\frac{1}{2}+\sqrt{3}\text{i})+(\frac{1}{2}+\sqrt{3}\text{i})(\frac{1}{2}-\sqrt{3}\text{i}) & =0 \\ {x}^{2}-\frac{x}{2}+x\sqrt{3}\text{i}-\frac{x}{2}-x\sqrt{3}\text{i}+\frac{1}{4}-3{\text{i}}^{2} & =0 \\ {x}^{2}-x+\frac{1}{4}+3 & =0 \\ {x}^{2}-x+\frac{13}{4} & =0\end{aligned}
$$

This equation has roots $x=\frac{1}{2}\pm \sqrt{3}\text{i},$ but the coefficient of ${x}^{2}$ is not $4.$ Therefore, to find the desired equation, we multiply the equation above by $4.$ This gives

$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}-x(6+8\text{i})-x(6-8\text{i})+(6-8\text{i})(6+8\text{i}) & =0 \\ {x}^{2}-6x-8x\text{i}-6x+8x\text{i}+36-64{\text{i}}^{2} & =0 \\ {x}^{2}-12x+36+64 & =0 \\ {x}^{2}-12x+100 & =0\end{aligned}

$$

$$
